{"agent_path":"019ffb63-6532-7850-b2f1-b1e6aed9bab0","status":{"completed":"## Chosen contract

```ts
requestGithubAppInstallationToken(
  input: {
    readonly subjectToken: string;
    readonly resource: string;
    readonly scope: string;
  },
): Promise<
  | {
      readonly ok: true;
      readonly accessToken: string;
      readonly expiresAt: string;
    }
  | {
      readonly ok: false;
      readonly error:
        | "invalid_request"
        | "invalid_target"
        | "invalid_scope"
        | "server_error"
        | "temporarily_unavailable";
    }
>
```

The broker must normalize `resource` and `scope`, authenticate the supplied OIDC subject token, evaluate the existing compiled Token Issuance Policy, and only then mint the repository-scoped GitHub App token.

The RPC must not accept an app selector, installation ID, private key, policy selector, audience override, or caller-controlled permissions object.

## Placement

- Public broker source owns the serializable types and shared typed operation, alongside the in-progress `packages/token-exchange` extraction.
- Deployment repo `src/worker.ts` owns the default `WorkerEntrypoint`, because it owns production policy and OIDC composition.
- `fetch(request: Request)` delegates to the existing HTTP handler, preserving `POST /token`, status codes, headers, and public compatibility.
- `cyspbot` invokes only `requestGithubAppInstallationToken`; its binding should be generated as a typed `Service`, not the current `Fetcher`.

## Rationale

A raw `fetch()` binding preserves behavior but is not a typed RPC. A low-level exchange mirror unnecessarily exposes OAuth protocol fields and creates a shallow interface.

The selected method is the smallest useful deep seam while retaining the existing subject-token authorization. An unrestricted method would create a confused deputy: possession of the service binding would become sufficient to mint tokens for caller-selected repositories and scopes.

The current inspection is sufficient to conclude the interface design, although implementation remains incomplete because the broker checkout has an in-progress token-exchange extraction with deleted old imports and untracked replacement files. No files were edited.

Thoroughly debate the implementation details of this change, in particular any identifiers that have been introduced and any configuration changes. List these with justifications or alternatives

The transport split is sound:

- Use CWI’s narrow `issueToken(audience)` RPC.
- Use the existing broker OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange endpoint through an internal service binding’s `.fetch()`.
- Do not add a second broker RPC API merely to avoid HTTP. Cloudflare service bindings support both HTTP and RPC without traversing the public Internet; HTTP is appropriate when the existing contract is already OAuth-based. [Service bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/), [HTTP service bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/http/), [RPC service bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/rpc/)

The current implementation is plumbing rather than a complete end-to-end feature: the root Worker does not yet call the helper, and the broker deployment has not yet registered the workload-identity issuer or added a matching permit policy.

## Identifiers

1. `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER`

Current binding name: [client config](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/wrangler.jsonc:13)

This is clear and capability-oriented: it says what the binding provides, not how it is transported.

Alternatives:

- `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_EXCHANGE` — more precise about the operation, but less clearly identifies the deployment.
- `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER_SERVICE` — explicit that this is a service binding, but leaks an implementation detail into application code.

Recommendation: keep `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER`. The name should not change merely because the broker uses HTTP rather than RPC.

2. `github-app-token-broker`

Current deployed Worker name: [broker config](/Users/cysp/src/github-app-token-broker-deploy/config/workers/github-app-token-broker.wrangler.json:1)

This is correct for the current single-production-Worker arrangement.

The important alternative is environment-qualified names:

- `github-app-token-broker-production`
- `github-app-token-broker-staging`

That becomes preferable once staging and production are separate Workers. Service bindings target a specific deployed Worker, and environment-qualified targets avoid accidentally giving staging access to production credentials.

3. `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_ISSUER`

Current binding name: [client config](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/wrangler.jsonc:19)

This matches the CWI deployment’s role and the existing smoke configuration. The drawback is that “issuer” can mean either:

- the binding to the issuer Worker; or
- the JWT `iss` claim, currently `https://workload-identity.chikachow.org`.

Alternatives:

- `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TOKEN_ISSUER` — clearer at the call site.
- `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_SERVICE` — transport-oriented, but loses the token-issuing meaning.

Recommendation: keep it if consistency with the CWI project is valuable, but document explicitly that this is a Worker binding, not the JWT issuer URL.

4. `workload-identity-issuer` and `WorkloadIdentityIssuer`

These are correctly separated:

- `workload-identity-issuer` is the deployment-global Worker name.
- `WorkloadIdentityIssuer` is the named RPC entrypoint and must exactly match the exported class. [CWI entrypoint](/Users/cysp/src/cloudflare-workload-identity/workers/workload-identity-issuer/src/index.ts:11)

The method `issueToken(audience: string)` is a good small interface. It avoids allowing the caller to choose the subject, signing key, issuer, or arbitrary claims. The binding properties control those values.

A stricter alternative would be `issueToken()` with no argument, since this particular binding has one allowed audience. That would make the interface safer, but would specialize the shared CWI Worker unnecessarily. The current wrapper already fixes the audience, so retaining the generic CWI method is reasonable.

5. `urn:chikachow:workload:cyspbot`

Current subject: [source config](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/wrangler.jsonc:24)

This is a good opaque authorization principal. It is more suitable for policy matching than a mutable display name.

The risk is cross-environment identity reuse. If staging or preview deployments use the same subject, they may become indistinguishable to the broker.

Alternatives:

- `urn:chikachow:workload:cyspbot:production`
- `urn:chikachow:workload:cyspbot:staging`
- `urn:chikachow:workload:cyspbot:preview:<id>`

Recommendation: the current value is acceptable for production-only deployment. Before introducing another environment, use environment-specific subjects and exact broker permits. The subject should not contain repository permissions or resource names; those belong in the broker policy.

6. `https://cyspbot.chikachow.org`

This value currently serves three roles:

- CWI `allowedAudiences`
- the client’s `githubAppTokenBrokerAudience`
- the broker’s `TOKEN_BROKER_AUDIENCE`

The current broker configuration confirms that value. [Broker audience](/Users/cysp/src/github-app-token-broker-deploy/config/workers/github-app-token-broker.wrangler.json:43)

Keeping it has a strong compatibility advantage. It is also valid to use a URL-shaped logical audience that does not identify the token endpoint itself.

Alternatives:

- `urn:chikachow:service:github-app-token-broker`
- `https://github-app-token-broker.chikachow.org`

A dedicated audience is conceptually cleaner because it distinguishes security identity from public routing. However, changing it requires coordinated changes to:

- CWI `allowedAudiences`
- client code
- broker `TOKEN_BROKER_AUDIENCE`
- broker permits and any other clients

Recommendation: keep the current audience for this change, but document it as a logical audience rather than an endpoint URL. Do not change it casually.

7. `https://cyspbot.chikachow.org/token`

Current endpoint: [client module](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/src/github-app-token.ts:8)

This is functionally valid and matches the broker’s existing route. The request still remains internal because it uses the service binding, not global `fetch`.

Alternatives:

- `https://github-app-token-broker/token`
- `https://token-broker.internal/token`

With an HTTP service binding, the binding selects the target Worker; the URL must be valid, but the public hostname should not be treated as the security boundary. [HTTP service bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/)

Recommendation: either retain the existing URL for contract clarity or use a clearly internal sentinel hostname. Do not derive authorization from the hostname. The `/token` path is the important handler contract.

8. `requestGitHubAppInstallationToken`

Current helper: [client module](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/src/github-app-token.ts:38)

The name hides the two-step mechanism, which is good. Callers should request a GitHub installation token, not know that the implementation first obtains a workload identity token.

Alternatives:

- `requestGitHubAppInstallationAccessToken` — more precise GitHub terminology.
- `exchangeWorkloadIdentityForGitHubAppToken` — exposes the mechanism and makes future changes harder.
- `getGitHubAppToken` — too vague; it hides that this performs network calls and may fail.

Recommendation: keep the current name unless the package is becoming a public library. If it does, `requestGitHubAppInstallationAccessToken` is the clearest public name. Also choose one repository-wide spelling convention: the new code uses brand-correct `GitHub`, while existing broker code contains `Github`.

9. `GitHubAppInstallationTokenRequest`

Current shape:

```ts
{
  resource: string;
  scope: string;
}
```

This is flexible and correctly leaves resource normalization and authorization to the broker.

The tradeoff is that every caller must understand OAuth resource syntax and GitHub permission scope syntax.

Alternatives:

- A typed `GitHubRepositoryResource` plus a permission union — better local safety, but duplicates broker-domain types.
- A capability-specific function such as `requestCyspbotRepositoryReadToken()` — strongest least privilege, but not reusable.
- A request with no resource or scope — simpler, but would encourage broad broker defaults.

Recommendation: retain the generic request if this is a reusable client. If the Worker only needs one known repository and permission set, expose a narrower capability-specific function instead. The final resource and scope must be decided before adding the broker Permit Statement; the current test values should not silently become production authorization.

10. `githubAppTokenBrokerAudience` and `githubAppTokenBrokerEndpoint`

Both are exported constants. [Constants](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/src/github-app-token.ts:5)

Exporting them makes them part of the package API. That is appropriate if other Workers are expected to consume the client package, but unnecessary if only the local Worker uses the helper.

Alternatives:

- Keep them private and export only the request function.
- Put the audience in a shared contract package.
- Generate client constants from deployment configuration.

Recommendation: keep the audience immutable and not caller-supplied. Consider making both constants private unless this package is intentionally a reusable client library. The audience should not be configurable through an untrusted request.

11. `GitHubAppTokenClientEnvironment`

The name describes an environment, but the value is really a dependency boundary containing two bindings.

`GitHubAppTokenClientBindings` or `GitHubAppTokenDependencies` would be more precise.

More importantly, this interface currently declares:

```ts
WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_ISSUER: unknown;
```

The generated environment declares the binding as generic `Service`, because Wrangler cannot infer the RPC type from the separately deployed Worker. [Generated bindings](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/src/env.generated.d.ts:1)

The runtime guard is defensible as a cross-deployment safety check, but `unknown` loses compile-time validation at precisely the security-sensitive boundary.

Alternatives:

- Publish a tiny type-only CWI contract package containing `issueToken()` and `{ token }`.
- Define a local `WorkloadIdentityIssuerBinding` and isolate one explicit adapter cast at the composition boundary.
- Generate types from a combined local configuration if the CWI source can be made available.
- Keep the runtime guard, but do not expose `unknown` as the public environment type.

Recommendation: use a narrow shared or local contract and confine any unavoidable cast to one adapter. Do not hand-edit the generated environment file; Cloudflare recommends generated binding types and intentional compatibility configuration. [Workers Best Practices](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/best-practices/workers-best-practices/)

12. `IssuedWorkloadIdentityToken`

The local `{ token: string }` shape is appropriately minimal, but its name should distinguish it from the GitHub access token.

Alternatives:

- `WorkloadIdentityToken`
- `WorkloadIdentityAssertion`
- `IssuedToken`, matching the CWI source

Recommendation: use `WorkloadIdentityToken` in the client-facing contract. `Assertion` may better express that it is an OIDC subject token and not an access token.

## Configuration

13. `remote: true`

Current in both source and private deployment config: [source](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/wrangler.jsonc:13), [deployment overlay](/Users/cysp/.codex/worktrees/cyspbot-deploy-workload-identity-20260814/config/workers/cyspbot.wrangler.jsonc:17)

This is the most concerning configuration choice. In Wrangler, `remote: true` primarily controls local development: it makes local `wrangler dev` use the deployed binding. It is not what makes a production service binding private or “remote.” [Local development and remote bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/local-development/)

With the current source config, a developer running locally could accidentally invoke the deployed CWI and broker and obtain real credentials.

Alternatives:

- Omit `remote` from normal source configuration and use local service workers or mocks.
- Create an explicit development environment with non-production Worker names and subjects.
- Require an intentional `wrangler dev --remote` workflow for deployed-service testing.
- Keep `remote: true` only in a clearly named production-integration configuration.

Recommendation: remove it from the public/default development config. Production service bindings do not need it. If remote integration testing is valuable, make that a separate explicit environment.

14. Production values in the public source configuration

The source file includes:

- production Worker names
- production subject
- production audience
- `remote: true`

But the documentation says the public Wrangler files contain only local-development and dry-run values. [Documentation](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/docs/implementation.md:39)

This creates two competing sources of truth: the source repository and the private deployment repository.

Alternatives:

- Source config owns binding names and local test targets; private deployment config owns production subjects, audiences, routes, and environment-qualified service names.
- Source config is deliberately production-owned; update the documentation and accept that it is deployment configuration.
- Generate both from a shared, reviewed deployment manifest.

Recommendation: use the first model. Identity-bearing `props` and environment-specific service targets belong in the deployment repository. If source config needs those fields for dry-run type generation, use explicit non-production values and ensure local execution cannot reach production.

15. `props.subject` and `props.allowedAudiences`

These correctly match the CWI entrypoint contract:

```json
{
  "subject": "...",
  "allowedAudiences": ["..."]
}
```

The array is a deliberate allow-list and is future-compatible with multiple broker audiences. A scalar `audience` would make accidental broadening harder, but would require changing the CWI contract.

Recommendation: retain the array because it matches the existing issuer API, but keep it one-element unless there is a concrete second audience. Adding another audience is an authorization change, not a harmless configuration edit.

16. Environment inheritance

If named Wrangler environments are added later, service bindings and their properties must be repeated deliberately; they should not be assumed to inherit safely. Cloudflare also requires the target Worker to be deployed before a service binding can invoke it. [Service bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/)

Recommended deployment order:

1. Ensure the CWI issuer deployment exists.
2. Deploy the broker with its CWI issuer registration and permit policy.
3. Deploy `cyspbot` with the matching binding configuration.
4. Run a real token-exchange smoke test that verifies the exact subject, audience, resource, and scope.

17. Broker-side issuer registration

The current broker deployment registers only GitHub Actions and Google providers. [Provider registrations](/Users/cysp/src/github-app-token-broker-deploy/src/oidc-provider-registrations.ts:1)

It does not yet trust `https://workload-identity.chikachow.org`. The broker also lacks a Permit Statement for the CWI subject in the current policy. [Token policy](/Users/cysp/src/github-app-token-broker-deploy/src/token-issuance-policy.ts:36)

This is a production blocker, not an optional follow-up. The broker must add:

- the exact CWI issuer URL;
- the appropriate generic JWT/OIDC profile;
- the exact subject constraint;
- the intended GitHub resource;
- the intended permission scope.

The service binding itself grants transport capability, not authorization. The broker policy must remain the final authorization boundary.

18. Compatibility date and flags

`compatibility_date` remains `2026-07-24` in both configurations. [Source config](/Users/cysp/src/cyspbot/workers/cyspbot/wrangler.jsonc:5)

Updating it to the current date may be appropriate under Cloudflare’s best practices, but it can change runtime behavior. I would not bundle that unrelated runtime change into this feature unless the project intentionally updates compatibility dates as part of every deployment.

The existing Node compatibility-disabled flags are reasonable for this code: the new client uses Web APIs and does not need Node shims. Do not add `nodejs_compat` merely because the binding is new.

## Interface and test concerns

19. Returning `Promise<Response>`

This preserves the broker’s existing OAuth success and error response exactly, which is useful for a forwarding handler.

It is shallow as a domain API: callers that need the token must parse the response themselves, and every caller must understand the broker’s wire format.

Alternatives:

- Return a typed `GitHubAppInstallationAccessToken`.
- Throw a typed broker error for OAuth failures.
- Return a discriminated success/error result.

Recommendation: use `Response` only if the caller will forward or deliberately own protocol parsing. Otherwise, return a typed result and centralize parsing in this module.

20. Actual call site

The root Worker currently exports the helper but does not invoke it. This means the change currently proves configuration and client plumbing, not token acquisition behavior.

That is acceptable if this is an intentional preparatory change. If the requirement is for `cyspbot` to request a token now, add the call in the actual internal handler that needs it. Do not expose the token through the public root route.

21. Test binding shape

The unit tests correctly exercise:

- fixed audience;
- standard RFC 8693 grant and token types;
- explicit resource and scope;
- failure before broker invocation when the issuer returns an invalid token.

However, the Miniflare integration mock for `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_ISSUER` is an HTTP `Response` mock, not an RPC object with `issueToken()`. It therefore does not verify the real named-entrypoint RPC contract. A small local CWI Worker or a deployment smoke test should cover that boundary.

Also, casting an empty object to the generated `CyspbotEnv` in existing Worker tests hides required-binding setup. That is harmless while the root Worker never touches the bindings, but should be replaced with a narrower test environment or real binding fixtures once the call site is added.

## Recommended final shape

1. Keep CWI RPC as:

   `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_ISSUER.issueToken(fixedBrokerAudience)`

2. Keep the broker’s existing OAuth endpoint over:

   `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER.fetch(.../token)`

3. Keep the standard RFC 8693 token-type identifiers and explicit scope.

4. Use a typed CWI contract rather than exposing `unknown`.

5. Decide whether the helper is a transport adapter returning `Response` or a domain client returning a typed access token.

6. Move production identity properties out of the public/default Wrangler config and remove ordinary `remote: true`.

7. Add the broker issuer registration and exact Permit Statement before calling this production-complete.

8. Decide the exact authorized repository and scope; do not let the generic request shape become an accidental broad capability.

No files were changed during this review.

Verify that workload identity token terminology, I don’t think it is an access token

You’re right: the CWI-issued credential is not an OAuth access token.

The accurate distinction is:

- CWI RPC result: a short-lived workload identity token/assertion, `IssuedToken { token }`. It is a signed JWT and is not issued by an OAuth token endpoint.
- Broker input: that credential is sent as RFC 8693 `subject_token`, with `subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token`. This describes the broker’s validation profile; it does not make the credential an OAuth access token. [RFC 8693 §2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.html#section-2.1)
- Broker output: the requested GitHub App Installation Access Token, requested with `requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token`. That is the actual OAuth bearer/access token. [RFC 8693 §2.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.html#section-2.2.1)

The CWI documentation confirms the preferred vocabulary: use “workload identity token” or “workload identity assertion” generally, and “OIDC ID token” only for this named consumer profile. [workload-identity-profile.md](/Users/cysp/src/cloudflare-workload-identity/docs/workload-identity-profile.md:23)

Our current docs mostly follow this correctly. One phrase in the client comment—“presents that token as an OIDC ID Token subject token”—is technically profile-accurate but ambiguous. A clearer wording would be:

## First experiment: `/cyspbot status` issue-comment reaction

When GitHub sends an authenticated `issue_comment` event whose body is exactly `/cyspbot status`, cyspbot adds an `eyes` reaction to that comment.

Why this is a good first slice:

- It belongs in the webhook receiver, where GitHub authentication already exists.
- The installation token is genuinely required: creating an issue reaction requires the GitHub App’s `Issues: write` permission. ([GitHub REST reactions](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/reactions/reactions))

The required configuration change is a narrowly scoped `issues:write` broker policy and GitHub App permission. The handler should derive a canonical repository resource only from the authenticated event, enforce the `chikachow` owner, and never accept arbitrary `scope` or `resource` values from HTTP input.

A weaker plumbing-only alternative is `GET /github/status`, which fetches the latest commit using the existing `contents:read` policy. GitHub documents that the commits endpoint accepts installation tokens with `Contents: read`. ([GitHub REST commits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits)) But for a public repository the token is not materially necessary, and a public route creates rate-limit and coupling concerns.

I would defer comments, labels, and automated PR analysis until the webhook processing has retry, deduplication, and failure handling. Avoid building a generic GitHub proxy entirely.
